title: 02 - Architectural Design
text:
Arclight’s architecture is built on a modular, cross-platform framework that prioritizes on-device execution to ensure absolute privacy for Protected Health Information (PHI) and independence from cloud infrastructure. The methodology for integrating machine learning capabilities into the application is divided into model development and front-end integration.


Below is a visual representation of the lifecycle of an Arclight ML module, from development to on-device output:





---
config:
  theme: neo
  look: neo
  layout: dagre
---
flowchart TD
    subgraph Model Development
        Dev("Pre-Training")
        Fine("Retrieval Fine-Tuning")
        Eval("Model Evaluation")
    end
    GPL("Deploy under GPL 3.0 license")
    subgraph Shiny POC
        UI("UI Mockup")
        Opt("Model Quantization and Optimization")
        Int("Model Integration")
        Dock("Dockerize")
    end
    subgraph Flutter Module
        Pre("Data Import & Preprocessing in Dart")
        Loc("Local Model Execution")
        Out("Output Formatting & Display")
    end
    Dev --> Fine
    Fine --> Eval
    Eval --> GPL
    Eval --> UI
    UI --> Opt
    Opt --> Int
    Int --> Dock
    Dock --> GPL
    Dock --> Pre
    Pre --> Loc
    Loc --> Out
    Out --> GPL









The core encoder retrieval model is adapted and optimized for local, low-latency execution on device.

Domain Focus: End-to-end domain specific training to optimize retrieval across keywords and semantic layers.
Export & Quantization: Export the model and retrieval pipelines into the open ONNX format, applying quantization to optimize memory usage and performance across desktop and mobile devices.




Prior to the full mobile and desktop rollout, a containerized prototype is constructed using Shiny to validate workflows and user experience:

Rapid Prototyping: Build a web-based proof-of-concept to test local language model processing and visual outputs with stakeholders.
Containerization: Package the Shiny interface and quantized ONNX runtime inside a Docker container to ensure reproducible testing across different evaluation environments.
Workflow Validation: Gather user feedback on interactive reporting features—including dynamic maps, tables, and epidemic curves—to refine UI/UX specifications before native app development.




The core application is built using the Flutter framework, enabling a single codebase to deploy across Android, Windows, and Linux. For the local model integration, a standardized process is followed within the Dart codebase:

Front-End Design: Develop the responsive front-end user interface components in Flutter to capture inputs (text, audio, images).
Data Import & Preprocessing: Write robust data ingestion and preprocessing handlers in Dart to prepare inputs for model compatibility.
Model Execution: Invoke the quantized ONNX model locally using cross-platform ONNX Runtime bindings in Dart to run inferences strictly on-device.
Output Formatting: Capture the inference results, process and format them (generating charts, tables, maps, or textual decision support), and display them within the UI.

This workflow ensures on-device reasoning and privacy preservation across all target platforms.

title: The Frontier Fallacy
text:
Why Healthcare Doesn’t Need Trillion-Parameter Models
When a health tech organization decides to implement artificial intelligence today, the default instinct is almost always to reach for the biggest cloud-hosted engine on the market. These massive, multi-billion and trillion-parameter frontier systems are engineering marvels, capable of composing sonnets, answering trivia, and simulating natural human banter. Yet when deployed into clinical environments, this broad capability introduces severe operational baggage. Healthcare workflows rarely demand an open-ended conversationalist; they require precise, repetitive execution across structured data tasks. Piped through external cloud APIs, these generalist giants saddle health systems with unpredictable monthly bills, noticeable seconds of network latency, and persistent regulatory anxiety over data exposure and HIPAA compliance. Paying for an ocean of world knowledge when you only need a pipeline to parse medical records is an expensive mismatch.

The path forward is not to abandon modern language processing, but to rethink its scale entirely. Rather than relying on massive cloud models designed to do everything passably well, engineering teams should turn toward small, specialized models featuring architectures under 3 billion parameters, and trained or tuned specifically on biomedical schemas and clinical terminology. Organizations do not need a model that knows 19th-century history to extract a patient’s symptom timeline or parse an unstructured lab intake form. By scoping the model’s linguistic focus strictly to the language of medicine and constraining its output to rigid formats like JSON, a compact engine running locally can easily out-execute a distant supercomputer. The path forward is to treat artificial intelligence like a purpose-built instrument rather than an unconstrained chatbot.
The business and operational returns of this architectural shift are immediate. Organizations that transition specialized tasks away from commercial cloud endpoints routinely see inferencing costs drop by more than 90%. Because small, specialized models are compact enough to run on dedicated, containerized internal hardware or local machines, per-token billing volatility is replaced with fixed, predictable compute expenses. Latency falls from seconds down to milliseconds, and structured output constraints virtually eliminate the formatting hallucinations common in chatty foundation models. Most importantly, sensitive protected health information never has to leave the local network, entirely eliminating the attack surface and compliance headaches of third-party cloud data transit.
Right-sizing your model architecture to match task complexity is an engineering and budgetary discipline, not a compromise. For AI systems deployed in healthcare settings,functional, reliable, and secure execution always wins.

title: Welcome to the Arclight Project
text:
Arclight is an open-source suite of NLP models designed to be deployed on device via a cross-platform app. Arclight is designed for use by epidemiologists, clinicians, and public health personnel investigating infectious disease outbreaks in novel populations and locations.
Whether the health emergency is a new outbreak of a bacterial infection, a novel virus, a drug-resistant fungus, an environmental toxin, or a bioterror attack, the first contact between pathogen and the public health system will be the outbreak investigation conducted by local health departments. The Arclight application provides front line public health professionals with actionable decision support based on the latest advances in local artificial intelligence.

title: Zero-Trust AI
text:
The Necessity for Offline Decision Support for Field Epidemiology
The most critical public health interventions rarely happen in sterile, climate-controlled environments equipped with fiber-optic internet. They unfold in rural clinics, remote border settlements, and post-disaster zones where a stable cellular connection is an unpredictable luxury. Despite this operational reality, the vast majority of modern data surveillance and clinical decision-support tools remain heavily tethered to the cloud. When developers build applications that require a continuous ping to a centralized server or a commercial artificial intelligence endpoint, they inadvertently build a glass cannon. The moment the local network drops or bandwidth throttles, the application immediately freezes. Epidemiologists and field nurses are instantly forced to abandon their digital ecosystems and revert to chaotic paper forms, manual transcription, and fragmented physical line-lists. This technological regression occurs during the exact moments when rapid, accurate data processing is most critical for outbreak containment and emergency resource allocation. A system that only operates smoothly under optimal infrastructure conditions is fundamentally broken for the realities of field medicine.
The architectural countermeasure to this systemic fragility is the deployment of local-first, quantized machine learning. Rather than relying on a distant, trillion-parameter supercomputer to process clinical narratives, health tech teams must architect pipelines capable of running entirely on standard, consumer-grade laptops and ruggedized edge hardware. This resilience is achieved through the use of “small” language models—compact, highly efficient engines typically under three billion parameters—that have been mathematically compressed to fit comfortably within the limited memory footprint of a standard field tablet. These models are explicitly stripped of generalized internet trivia and open-ended conversational fluff. Instead, they are strictly specialized and tuned for the precise extraction of medical symptoms, exposure timelines, geographic risk factors, and demographic variables from unstructured text. By housing this computational intelligence directly on the physical hardware, the application becomes completely self-sufficient. It parses messy field interviews, structures the raw data into rigid, analytical formats, and cross-references jurisdictional case definitions without ever making a single call to a remote server.

Shifting this computational burden directly to the edge fundamentally transforms both the reliability and security of field operations. Epidemiologists can synthesize complex triage logs and generate structured, actionable data at the point of care with zero interruption. The diagnostic and analytical work continues seamlessly, entirely immune to regional network blackouts or degraded local infrastructure. Beyond this immediate operational continuity, the disconnected architecture solves one of the most persistent and expensive bottlenecks in global medical technology: data privacy and regulatory compliance. Because the artificial intelligence inference happens entirely locally on the device, it establishes a true zero-trust privacy perimeter. Sensitive patient details, identifiable demographic markers, and protected health information never leave the local hard drive. By physically eliminating the transit of data to third-party cloud providers, health organizations eradicate massive compliance hurdles, eliminate recurring remote toll costs, and close severe cyber vulnerabilities, achieving absolute, uncompromised data residency by default.
True operational resilience dictates that critical surveillance systems must remain fully functional when the external network inevitably goes down. Building sustainable, scalable artificial intelligence for public health requires treating internet connectivity as an unpredictable variable, not a baseline engineering guarantee.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Practical implementation of machine learning and artificial intelligence is significantly lacking on the front lines of public health. While many proposed solutions show promise in controlled academic settings, actual implementation is challenged by data fragmentation, data bias, privacy concerns, domain oversights, or a reliance on computing infrastructure unavailable to under-resourced local health departments.
Whether the health emergency is a new outbreak of an existing pathogen, a novel virus, a drug-resistant fungus, an environmental toxin, or a bioterror attack, the first contact between pathogen and the public health system will be the outbreak investigation conducted by local health departments. The impact generated by aiding this process with ML/AI tools is considerable, and currently unaddressed.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Our Solution
Arclight is an open-source suite of NLP models designed to empower epidemiologists and public health professionals with real-time decision support during outbreak investigations. The models are designed to run locally, on device via a cross-platform app, replicating the functionality of the latest foundation models, but without the possibility of hallucination, PHI leakage, or data contamination.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Design Goals and Exclusions
Arclight will assist field epidemiologists and public health professionals when investigating potential infectious disease outbreaks. Arclight will exclusively process information on-device to protect PHI, eliminate infrastructure costs, and add direct oversight by the end-user.
Specific Arclight functions will evolve over time, but will generally will be designed to support epidemiologists during the following phases of an outbreak investigation:

Integrating existing public health surveillance data
Processing case reports and investigative notes
Refining the case definition based on collected information and alternative diagnoses
Organizing case reports based on population, location, and time
Developing etiological hypotheses based on observed notes and reference data.

Arclight deployment will include only Android, Linux, and Windows devices. Model performance will be constrained by the demands of on-device processing, to include available modules in the required tech stack. Arclight will not replace established decision support tools used for policy development, outbreak forecasting, or other use cases requiring large data sets and server-grade processing power; rather, it fills a gap at the local level.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Note



Arclight follows principles of MVP development and separation of concerns. The main Arclight model will be the initial release, developed, optimized, and made available in a standalone ONNX format. A quantized version will then be developed as an integrated Shiny app packaged in a deployable Docket container. The fully integrated Flutter application will be the final release, initially targeting Android, Windows, and Linux systems.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 1: Model Development & Optimization
Train, validate, and optimize machine learning models before exporting for on-device execution, publishing source code under an open-source license.

Tasks:

Baseline Model Development: Develop, train, and validate initial model
Optimization & Quantization: Apply post-training quantization and model compression techniques to minimize memory footprint and optimize execution speed for target end-user devices.
ONNX Export: Export tuned models into the industry standard ONNX format required for widespread mobile and desktop release.
Open-Source Licensing: Host model source code and assets on GitHub under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPL v3.0).

title: 01 - Development Plan
section: Phase 2: UI/UX Proof of Concept (Shiny & Docker)
text:
Phase 2: UI/UX Proof of Concept (Shiny & Docker)
Prototype the user interface and validate operational workflows quickly through a web-based Proof of Concept (POC).

Tasks:

Shiny Prototype: Build a functional Shiny interface to mock up layouts, data ingestion workflows, and visualization formats required for different end-use cases.
Workflow Validation: Test end-to-end data processing, user interaction flows, and structured decision-support outputs within the Shiny workspace.
Docker Containerization: Package the Shiny application into a Docker container for isolated testing, streamlined sharing, and collecting feedback from epidemiologists and stakeholders.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 3: Flutter Application Development & Integration
Construct the production cross-platform native application framework and integrate local machine learning models into the Dart pipeline.

Tasks:

App Scaffolding & Front-End: Develop responsive front-end UI components in Flutter supporting Android, Linux, and Windows targeting cross-platform consistency.
Dart Data Pipeline: Implement data import, sanitization, and preprocessing functions in Dart to prepare user inputs for model consumption.
On-Device Model Integration: Integrate exported .onnx models into the Flutter application for privacy-preserving, local execution.
Secure Local Storage: Implement encrypted local databases (e.g., SQLite or Hive) with local encrypted backups to external storage media like USB drives.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 4: Integration Testing & Multi-Platform Deployment
Conduct rigorous system-wide testing and publish production application builds across supported platforms and repositories.

Tasks:

Integration Testing: Perform comprehensive integration testing across Android, iOS, and Windows, verifying on-device model accuracy, UI responsiveness, PHI censoring algorithms during PDF/CSV exports, and database security.
App Store & Open-Source Distribution: Publish finalized production binaries to app stores (Google Play Store, Apple App Store, Microsoft Store) and release full source code and build distributions on GitHub.
